claims.text: An integrated machine-learning interatomic potential can reliably estimate fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties in elemental, binary, and multicomponent high-entropy systems.
The potential will be trained using ab initio free-energy data incorporating vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration coupling contributions.
The proposed method will cost substantially less than full ab initio molecular dynamics.
Active learning will selectively invoke full ab initio molecular dynamics in regions where surrogate-model uncertainty is high.
The initial training domain will include Al, Cu, and Cu–Ni.
The method is planned to extend to high-entropy compositions such as CoCrFeMnNi.
The intended temperature domain extends from approximately 0.5Tm to temperatures above melting.
A learned potential-energy surface augmented with free-energy corrections mediates between atomic configurations and thermodynamic properties.
The added corrections account for harmonic and anharmonic vibrational contributions and electron–vibration coupling.
Training on ab initio free-energy components enables the ML potential to interpolate the complex free-energy landscape efficiently.
Active-learning sampling minimizes the amount of full ab initio molecular dynamics required.
The method preserves the fidelity of vibrational entropy and anharmonic corrections in both solid and liquid phases.
TOR-TILD provides relevant elemental and binary free-energy datasets that can be leveraged for training.
The method is expected to reduce computational cost by roughly one order of magnitude relative to full ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows.
Predicted phase free energies will agree with explicit molecular-dynamics results within a few percent.
Predicted latent heats will agree with explicit molecular-dynamics results within a few percent.
Preliminary evidence from elemental and binary systems is promising.
Performance in highly multicomponent high-entropy systems and under extreme conditions remains unvalidated.
Deviation exceeding approximately 5% from full ab initio molecular dynamics for elemental or binary systems will falsify the hypothesis.
Deviation exceeding approximately 10% from full ab initio molecular dynamics for high-entropy systems will falsify the hypothesis.
